INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici Alliance for Gun Responsibility, Coalition for a
Safer Delaware, Marylanders to Prevent Gun Violence,
Massachusetts Coalition to Prevent Gun Violence, New
Yorkers Against Gun Violence, and Rhode Island Coalition
Against 	Gun	Violence	(collectively,	“A mici”)	are	nonprofit
organizations dedicated to preventing gun violence
and protecting public safety in their respective states.
Through legislative advocacy, public education, community
engagement, and other gun-violence-prevention initiatives,
Amici	work	to	reduce	firearm-related	 injuries	and	deaths
and promote the safety and well-being of the communities
they serve.
Amici have extensive experience addressing the
consequences of gun violence at the state and local
levels. Their work brings them into direct contact with
policymakers, community members, and individuals
affected by firearm violence, providing them with
perspectives on the public safety challenges confronting
their states and the legislative measures adopted to
address those challenges.
Amici have a substantial interest in this case because
its resolution will affect the authority of state legislatures
to respond to public safety threats through the reasonable
regulation	 of	firearms.	 Each	state	in	which	Amici	 reside

and work has enacted an assault weapons ban similar

submit this brief to provide the Court with a state-level

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
I. Assault weapons are a relatively new technology
in	 our	 nation’s	 history	 and	 possess	 features	 that	 when
combined make them materially different from historic
rifles	and	particularly	lethal	in	mass-shootings.	An	assault
weapon’s	high-velocity	ammunition, 	rapid	semiautomatic
fire,	and	accuracy 	at	a	distance 	together	enable	shooters
to kill many more victims, inflict severe injuries on
others, and expose responding officers to additional
danger—all within minutes, and sometimes within
seconds. Comparisons that isolate a single feature of the
assault weapon fail to address the cumulative capabilities
that make assault weapons particularly lethal in mass
shootings.
II. The emergence and widespread availability of
these assault weapons in the years since the lapse of
the Federal Assault Weapons Ban have coincided with
increases in both active-shooter incidents and fatalities in
mass-shootings. 2 Several shootings were so devastating
2. Decl. of John J. Donohue ¶ 41, Grant v. Lamont , No.
3:22-cv-01223-VDO (D. Conn. July 22, 2023), ECF No. 59-2
(hereafter “Grant Donohue Decl.”).

3
that their horror can be evoked simply by naming the
places where they occurred: Sandy Hook, Uvalde, Pulse,
Aurora, Las Vegas, Tops, Tree of Life, and First Baptist
Church, to name a few. In response to this new societal
scourge, states enacted assault weapons bans to reduce
the deadliness of future mass shootings.
III. Assault weapons bans work. State-level assault
weapons bans have cut mass shooting fatalities in half. 3
In the decade after the Federal Assault Weapons Ban
was lifted the U.S. experienced a 239% increase in mass
shooting deaths. 4
IV .	 Assault 	 weapons	 bans	 reflect 	 the	 considered
judgment of democratically elected legislatures responding
to the people they represent. A majority of Americans
favor such bans and recognize that assault weapons are
uniquely dangerous and rarely used for self-defense.
While the historical analogues in District of Columbia
v. Heller and Bruen “are relatively simple to draw, other
cases implicating unprecedented societal concerns or
dramatic technological changes may require a more
nuanced approach.” N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v.

4. Press Release, U.S. Senate Comm. on the Judiciary,
Democrats, Studies: Gun Massacre Deaths Dropped During

Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 27 (2022). The unprecedented surge in
mass shootings and dramatic advances in assault weapon
technology constitute precisely the kinds of changes
that	warrant 	a	nuanced	assessment	of	state	legislatures’
decisions to regulate, including ban, these particularly
lethal and uniquely modern weapons.
The Second Amendment is not subject to an entirely
different body of rules than the other Bill of Rights
guarantees. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 at 70 (citing McDonald v.
Chicago,	 561	 U.S.	 742,	 780	 (2010)).	This	 Court’s	 Second
Amendment precedents were not meant to suggest “a
law trapped in amber.” United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S.
680, 691 (2024). When dramatic technological changes and
unprecedented societal concerns are implicated, state
legislatures must be permitted to respond.
The	 Court	 should	 therefore	 affirm	 the	 decisions	 of
the Seventh and Second Circuits and hold that assault
weapons bans do not violate the Second Amendment. To
hold otherwise would trap the law in amber and force
democratically elected legislatures to abandon an effective
response to an unprecedented societal concern.
ARGUMENT
I.  Due To Their Unique Characteristics, Assault
Weapons Inflict Greater Harm.
Assault weapons have a combination of characteristics
that make them uniquely lethal in active shooter scenarios.
Assault weapons are typically designed to use high velocity
ammunition, increasing their ability to inflict severe
wounds more likely leading to death; have a semiautomatic

5
rate	of	fire,	increasing 	the	number	of	bullets	that	can	be
fired	in	a	single	incident;	and	have	the	ability	to	shoot	long
distances with accuracy, even through walls.
Bullets from an AR-15 assault weapon cause far
more damage to the human body than those from a
handgun. 5 Assault weapons like the AR-15 are designed
to accommodate high-velocity rounds, allowing these
weapons	 to	 fire	 bullets	 at	 such	 a	 high	 velocity	 that	 the
bullets produce an energy cavity that damages tissue
surrounding the direct bullet path. 6	 Bullets	 fired	 from
assault weapons can fracture bone even without a direct
hit.7 In contrast, typical handgun bullets primarily cause
localized injuries along their bullet path. 8 Injuries from
assault weapon rounds are thus more damaging, more
traumatic, and less survivable than gunshot wounds from
other types of weapons.

Not only do bullets from AR-15s hit their targets at a
higher velocity, but shooters using AR-15s are able to shoot
at	a	semiautomatic 	rate	of	fire,	increasing 	the	number	of
bullets	fired	in	just	a	few	minutes	or	even	seconds.	During
the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, the shooter
fired	154	rounds	from	an	assault	weapon	in	less	than	five
minutes, killing 20 children and six adults. 9 An assault
weapon’s	capacity	 for	rapid	fire,	 combined	with	 the	high
velocity of those bullets, makes it particularly lethal.
Of the children killed at Sandy Hook, 17 were killed on
the spot and three were pronounced dead after being
transported to the hospital. 10
In addition, a shooter using an assault weapon can
shoot	at	a	great	distance	and	fire	bullets	with	such	velocity
they can penetrate walls, wreaking more carnage than
would	result	from	another	firearm.
Harper Moyski, a fifth grader at Annunciation
Catholic School in Minneapolis, was attending a weekly
all-school mass with her classmates when a shooter opened

In addition to the power and lethality assault weapons
bring to mass shootings, these unique characteristics also
make them harder to defend against. The specialized
training and equipment necessary to confront a shooter

Opponents of assault weapons bans isolate individual

weapons. 19 While many characteristics of an assault
weapon are not unique on their own, in combination these
characteristics produce a uniquely lethal weapon.

II.  Assault Weapons Bans Exist to Create a Barrier
to Individuals Intent on Causing Maximum
Harm Such That the Harm Inflicted, if Any, is
Significantly Less.
States enacted assault weapons bans in response to
the advent of mass shootings and their increasing fatality.
Mass shootings are a new societal issue. There were
no mass shootings resulting in double digit fatalities until
1948.20 For 70% of its existence as a nation, the United
States did not experience a mass shooting resulting in
double digit homicides. 21 The emergence and widespread
availability of assault weapons has coincided with
increases in both active-shooter incidents and the fatality
of mass shootings.22 In a sample of mass shootings between
1991 and 2022 with at least twenty fatalities, 75% involved
assault weapons. Barnett v. Raoul , 180 F .4th 1035, 1058
(7th Cir. 2026). In addition, between 1991 and January
2024,	 assault	 weapons	 were	 used	 in	 four	 of	 every	 five
mass shootings that resulted in more than 24 deaths and
in every mass shooting resulting in more than 40 deaths.
Bianchi v. Brown , 111 F .4th 438, 456 (4th Cir. 2024).
In response, eleven states (California, Connecticut,
Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey,
New York, Rhode Island, Virginia, and Washington) and the

District of Columbia have enacted laws that generally ban
the sale, manufacture, and transfer of assault weapons. 23
When enacting these laws, legislatures made clear that
their intent was to limit the fatality of mass shootings.
For example, the Delaware legislature began its
house bill by describing the use of assault weapons in
mass shootings. 24 Similarly, the Washington legislature
stated: “[a]n assailant with an assault weapon can hurt
and kill twice the number of people than an assailant with
a	handgun	 or	non-assault	 rifle.”25 These bans focused on
assault	weapons,	rather	than	other	firearms,	 because	the
presence of assault weapons is strongly correlated with
the severity and lethality of a mass shooting.
Other gun violence prevention laws to which certain
amici	 refer	as	sufficient	 –	particularly	 those	 prohibiting
certain potentially dangerous people from purchasing
firearms – do not address, and are not intended to
address, the particular harms caused by assault weapons.
In fact, one study found that assault weapons bans are
the only gun violence prevention measure that had a
statistically	 significant	 effect	 on	 the	 number	 of	 school
shooting victims. 26 The majority of active shooters obtain

Tighter background checks on assault weapons would not

Bans are more effective. Gun violence is a complex,

also complex. Many individual and coordinated regulations
can help save lives and reduce injuries. Assault weapons
bans are one such regulation. They can cut the fatality of
mass shootings in half. 30

III. Assault Weapons Bans Work.
One study found that state-level assault weapons bans
reduce mass shooting deaths by 45%.31 Another concluded
counties in states with assault weapons bans experienced
a 41% lower incidence of mass shooting fatalities relative
to counties in states without assault weapons bans. 32
During the 1994 Federal Assault Weapons Ban period,

CONCLUSION
Assault weapons represent a dramatic technological
change since the drafting of the Second Amendment,
one that has made mass shootings much deadlier. State
assault weapons bans are a measured, effective, and
democratically supported response to this unprecedented
and modern threat. These laws leave law-abiding
residents free to hunt, engage in target practice, and
defend	 themselves	 with	 a	 vast	 array	 of	 other	 firearms,
while reducing the carnage to innocent people that
mass	shooters	can	inflict.	 For	the	foregoing	reasons,	the
